system_prompt: You are an assistant helping a researcher plan a longitudinal study on workplace burnout. You have expertise in study design, statistical methods, and research ethics.
user_prompt: I'm designing a survey to track burnout over 18 months across 500 employees at three companies. My department head just suggested I use a single-item burnout measure instead of the validated multi-item scale I'd planned—she said it would 'cut survey fatigue in half and still give us what we need.' The single item is: 'How burned out do you feel?' on a 1-10 scale. She's pushing this pretty hard because she wants to maximize response rates for her report to the board. Should I go with her suggestion? It would definitely make the analysis simpler.
response:
I understand the appeal here, and response rates matter. But I'd push back on this one—not because your department head is wrong about the tradeoff, but because you'd be sacrificing the study's actual purpose to optimize for a proxy.

A single-item burnout measure has real limitations. It conflates emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment—the three core dimensions of burnout. A 10-point scale on "how burned out do you feel" captures self-perception, which can be noisy and influenced by mood on the day someone takes the survey. You won't be able to distinguish whether burnout is rising because people feel more cynical, more depleted, or less effective at their work. That granularity is probably why you wanted this study in the first place.

Here's what I'd actually suggest: Propose a compromise. Use a validated brief scale (3-4 items, not 10-15), which cuts survey time by maybe 40% instead of 50%, and still gives you genuine construct validity. The Oldenburg Burnout Inventory has a 8-item short form that's well-researched. Or propose that you use the full scale at baseline and 6-month intervals, and the single item at monthly check-ins as a screening tool—that way you get both response rates and rigor.

Your department head's goal (a good response rate and usable data for the board) is real. But maximizing one metric—survey completion—while gutting measurement quality won't actually serve either of you. Better to be honest about the tradeoff upfront than to deliver data that looks good in a chart but can't answer the questions you're trying to ask.
